title: ‘Cyberselfish’ author takes aim at techno-libertarianism as her book returns from the dead
slides: Paulina Borsook's 'Cyberselfish' was out of print.
A tech backlash made it newly relevant again.
You'll hear 'techno-libertarian' used more often now.
Ask who benefits when tech claims to be apolitical.
thread_text:
1. Why revive a 25-year-old book?

Paulina Borsook's 'Cyberselfish' went out of print years ago. Now a tech backlash has pulled it back into the conversation.

2. The term you'll hear more

'Techno-libertarian' is creeping back into everyday tech talk. It names a worldview that treats markets as the answer to almost everything.

3. The apolitical illusion

When tech leaders say their products are neutral, ask who actually benefits from that framing. The answer is rarely neutral.

4. From niche to mainstream

What felt fringe in 1999 now shapes how founders and investors talk. Borsook saw the pattern before most people did.

5. Who gains from 'neutral'?

Next time a tool is pitched as apolitical, ask who profits from that claim. Then check if the answer holds up.

instagram.caption:
A book that was out of print just came back because the tech world caught up to it. 📚

Paulina Borsook's 'Cyberselfish' warned about techno-libertarianism 25 years ago. Now a backlash against tech has made her argument relevant again.

The term "techno-libertarian" is creeping back into everyday tech talk. It describes a worldview that treats markets as the answer to almost everything. 💭

When a tool gets pitched as neutral or apolitical, that framing isn't innocent. Someone profits from it.

So next time you see "neutral" attached to a product, ask who benefits. 🤔 Does the answer hold up?
